evidence: update-product.dto.ts: UpdateProductDto checks only shape and types (@IsOptional/@IsString/@IsNumber) and holds no business rules.
update-product.command.ts: UpdateProductCommand(productId, dto) only copies the DTO fields. It adds no logic.
update-product.service.ts: UpdateProductService.execute builds new UpdateProductCommand(productId, dto) and calls commandBus.execute. It goes through the module's command, not around it.

update-product.command-handler.ts: UpdateProductCommandHandler.execute leaves invariants to Name.create/Description.create/Price.create and to product.isValid/brokenRules. It throws BrokenRulesException rather than re-validating inline.
All four files are about the single update-product use case. There is no unrelated concern.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
All four files serve one concern: the update-product use case. They form one linear CQRS flow. UpdateProductDto is the transport contract. UpdateProductService turns it into an UpdateProductCommand and sends it on the CommandBus. UpdateProductCommand copies the DTO fields. UpdateProductCommandHandler loads the product, applies the changes through the domain value objects and entity methods, checks the entity's broken rules, saves the product and publishes its events.

No rule is duplicated. The DTO checks only types and optionality (class-validator). The business invariants live in the value objects (Name.create, Description.create, Price.create) and in product.isValid/brokenRules. The handler calls those rather than restating them. The module's own abstractions are also used consistently: the service builds UpdateProductCommand through its constructor and dispatches it via the bus, without calling the handler directly.

The handler injects the concrete ProductRepository from infrastructure. That is an import-direction question, which is out of scope. The truthy checks (`if (price)` skips a price of 0) are a correctness issue, not a cohesion or boundary problem.
